items.stem: Which term describes lack of money and the physical necessities of life, such as adequate housing, food and resources?
items.answer: Material deprivation
items.markingKey: Material deprivation: lack of money and the physical necessities of life, such as adequate housing, food and resources. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “digital divide”? Give one example.
items.answer: The gap between those who have access to computers and the internet and those who do not. Example: pupils without home internet struggling with online homework.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the gap between those who have access to computers and the internet and those who do not); 1 mark for a relevant example such as pupils without home internet struggling with online homework. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “relative poverty” and “fear of debt”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Relative poverty: having an income well below the average for the society, so that people cannot afford a normal standard of living (e.g. a household with less than 60% of median income). Fear of debt: reluctance to take on loans for higher education, more common among working-class students (e.g. a student choosing a local course to avoid student loans).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A secondary school in Seoul finds that pupils eligible for free meals miss more school trips and have higher absence rates. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: achievement differences reflect class inequality: working-class pupils face material disadvantage and a middle-class school culture that rewards cultural capital, so schools reproduce rather than reduce inequality (Bourdieu, Bowles and Gintis).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Priya, aged 14, lives with five family members in a two-room flat in Auckland, often skips breakfast and has no computer at home. Explain how a New Right sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: state education is inefficient and does not meet the needs of the economy; competition, parental choice and a market in schools will raise standards (Chubb and Moe), while education should transmit a shared national culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Priya, a sociology student, is designing a project on the effects of poverty on pupils’ achievement. Evaluate the use of longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can follow children through their education into adulthood; they show how people’s lives change over time and allow cause and effect to be explored. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; being studied repeatedly may change participants’ behaviour. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of poverty on pupils’ achievement but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the hidden costs of education, such as uniforms, trips and equipment, which burden poorer families?
items.answer: Cost of free schooling
items.markingKey: Cost of free schooling: the hidden costs of education, such as uniforms, trips and equipment, which burden poorer families. [1]

items.stem: Daniel is planning a study of working-class students’ decisions about university. Explain two strengths of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) for this research.
items.answer: 1. They show how people themselves understood their experiences. 2. They give an insight into people’s feelings and meanings in their own words, so validity can be high.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to working-class students’ decisions about university. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes the theory that some groups lack the norms, values, skills and knowledge needed for educational success?
items.answer: Cultural deprivation
items.markingKey: Cultural deprivation: the theory that some groups lack the norms, values, skills and knowledge needed for educational success. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “cultural capital”? Give one example.
items.answer: Bourdieu’s term for the knowledge, attitudes, values, language and tastes that give advantages in education. Example: familiarity with books, museums and academic language.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Bourdieu’s term for the knowledge, attitudes, values, language and tastes that give advantages in education); 1 mark for a relevant example such as familiarity with books, museums and academic language. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “elaborated code” and “restricted code”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Elaborated code: Bernstein’s term for a speech code with a wider vocabulary and context-free meanings, associated with the middle class and used in schools (e.g. detailed explanations that do not depend on context). Restricted code: Bernstein’s term for a speech code with limited vocabulary and context-bound meanings, associated with the working class (e.g. short sentences assuming shared understanding).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A working-class pupil in Muscat says she feels “out of place” in lessons where teachers use long words and refer to books she has never read. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Priya’s parents in Seoul, both university lecturers, take her to museums, discuss news at dinner and help her choose challenging books. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A working-class pupil in Istanbul says she feels “out of place” in lessons where teachers use long words and refer to books she has never read. Explain how Marxist and liberal feminist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: achievement differences reflect class inequality: working-class pupils face material disadvantage and a middle-class school culture that rewards cultural capital, so schools reproduce rather than reduce inequality (Bourdieu, Bowles and Gintis). Liberal feminism: education has helped reduce gender inequality through equal opportunities policies, but stereotyping, subject choice and the hidden curriculum still steer girls and boys in different directions.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the influence of parents’ cultural activities on children’s achievement. Evaluate the use of unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; the interviewer can follow up answers and explore meanings in the interviewee’s own words. Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the influence of parents’ cultural activities on children’s achievement but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful case studies are for studying working-class pupils’ experiences of a high-achieving school.
items.answer: Strengths: they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised; the researcher’s interpretation may be biased. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying working-class pupils’ experiences of a high-achieving school but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Mohammed is planning a study of working-class pupils’ experiences of a high-achieving school. Explain one strength and one limitation of using semi-structured interviews for this study.

items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of working-class pupils’ experiences of a high-achieving school. [4]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “educational triage”, and give one example.
items.answer: Sorting pupils into those who will pass anyway, those who can be helped to pass and hopeless cases. Example: extra help for pupils on the grade borderline.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (sorting pupils into those who will pass anyway, those who can be helped to pass and hopeless cases); 1 mark for a relevant example such as extra help for pupils on the grade borderline. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “educational triage” and “setting”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Educational triage: sorting pupils into those who will pass anyway, those who can be helped to pass and hopeless cases (e.g. extra help for pupils on the grade borderline). Setting: grouping pupils by ability for particular subjects (e.g. a pupil in the top set for maths but the middle set for English).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A school in Auckland places pupils into sets in their first week, largely on the basis of a short test and teachers’ impressions; most pupils in the bottom set are from the poorest housing estate. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: labelling reflects and reproduces wider class inequality: teachers’ judgements are shaped by middle-class norms, and policies such as league tables encourage triage that disadvantages working-class pupils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A school in Doha places pupils into sets in their first week, largely on the basis of a short test and teachers’ impressions; most pupils in the bottom set are from the poorest housing estate. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: setting by ability is a meritocratic way of matching teaching to pupils’ abilities and allocating them to appropriate roles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.answer: Strengths: they may use several methods, increasing validity; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised; the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ experiences of being in a bottom set but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) to research pupils’ experiences of being in a bottom set.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they may be the only source of evidence about the past. Limitations: they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably; they are usually unrepresentative because only some people keep or publish them. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ experiences of being in a bottom set but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “ideal pupil”.
items.answer: The image of the perfect pupil that teachers use to judge pupils, often based on middle-class norms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the image of the perfect pupil that teachers use to judge pupils, often based on middle-class norms. [1]

items.stem: Rosenthal and Jacobson argued that teachers’ expectations can produce a self-fulfilling prophecy in pupils’ achievement. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: In their field experiment, randomly selected “spurters” made greater IQ gains, apparently because teachers expected more of them. Criticism: Replication attempts have produced mixed results, and the study involved deception.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Priya is planning a study of how teachers decide which set pupils are placed in. Explain one limitation of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how teachers decide which set pupils are placed in. [2]

Functionalism: setting by ability is a meritocratic way of matching teaching to pupils’ abilities and allocating them to appropriate roles.

items.stem: A survey of 1000 pupils aged 12 in Lisbon produced the data below. Table: percentage of pupils placed in each mathematics set | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Top set | 44% | 25%. Middle set | 31% | 29%. Bottom set | 25% | 46%. (a) Calculate the difference between Top set and Middle set for Middle-class pupils and for Working-class pupils, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that setting is the main reason for class differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) Middle-class pupils: 13 percentage points; Working-class pupils: 4 percentage points; the difference is larger for Middle-class pupils. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Working-class pupils than for Middle-class pupils among Bottom set; the figure is lower for Working-class pupils than for Middle-class pupils among Top set, Middle set; Bottom set had the highest figure for Working-class pupils. Educational triage and setting decisions reflect pressure on results. Qualifications: Set placement may reflect earlier attainment shaped by out-of-school factors; setting may follow rather than cause differences; some working-class pupils reach top sets. The data also come from official statistics of 1000 pupils aged 12 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (13 and 4); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: National data for Riyadh (240 pupils) show the following results. Table: percentage achieving five good passes at age 16 | 2015 | 2025. Pupils eligible for free school meals | 37% | 38%. Other pupils | 63% | 68%. (a) Suppose 200 of the respondents were Other pupils. Using the 2025 figure, calculate how many of them gave this response. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that material deprivation is the main cause of class differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) 68% of 200 = 68 ÷ 100 × 200 = 136 (to the nearest whole person). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Pupils eligible for free school meals, Other pupils; Other pupils had the highest figure for 2025. Labelling and setting may disadvantage poorer pupils. Qualifications: Free school meal eligibility is only a rough measure of class; cultural and in-school factors also matter; some poor pupils achieve highly. The data also come from official statistics of 240 pupils aged 16 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark method (68 ÷ 100 × 200); 1 mark answer 136. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are for studying the effects of poverty on pupils’ achievement.
items.answer: Strengths: they can follow children through their education into adulthood; comparing the same people at different points avoids the problem of comparing different samples. Limitations: sample attrition (people dropping out) can make the sample unrepresentative over time; they are very expensive and results take many years to appear. Theory: longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce mainly quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of poverty on pupils’ achievement but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: State one way in which middle-class parents may use cultural capital to help their children.
items.answer: Using educated language that matches school expectations.

items.stem: Douglas argued that working-class parents placed less value on education and showed less interest in their children’s progress. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Douglas’s longitudinal study found children whose parents showed less interest (measured by parents’ evening attendance) did less well. Criticism: Blackstone and Mortimore argued working-class parents may work longer or unsocial hours and feel uncomfortable in schools.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Functionalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.answer: 1. The interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part. 2. The interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the influence of parents’ cultural activities on children’s achievement. [4]

items.stem: Leila, a sociology student, found the following figures in a report on cultural capital and achievement in Jakarta. The report was based on 600 pupils aged 15. Table: percentage achieving high grades in an English exam | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Pupils who read for pleasure daily | 71% | 58%. Pupils who never read for pleasure | 56% | 50%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Pupils who read for pleasure daily. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that cultural capital explains class differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) 58 − 71 = -13 percentage points (Working-class pupils compared with Middle-class pupils). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Working-class pupils than for Middle-class pupils among Pupils who read for pleasure daily, Pupils who never read for pleasure; Pupils who read for pleasure daily had the highest figure for Working-class pupils. Reading for pleasure develops vocabulary and cultural capital valued by schools (Sullivan). Qualifications: Reading helps both classes, but class differences remain even among readers, suggesting material and school factors also matter; self-reported reading may be inaccurate. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 600 pupils aged 15 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 71 and 58; 1 mark for 13 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Explain how setting and streaming may disadvantage working-class pupils.

(a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Top set. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of social class and setting. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that setting is the main reason for class differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) 32 − 50 = -18 percentage points (Working-class pupils compared with Middle-class pupils). (b) They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Working-class pupils than for Middle-class pupils among Middle set, Bottom set; the figure is lower for Working-class pupils than for Middle-class pupils among Top set; Middle set had the highest figure for Working-class pupils. Educational triage and setting decisions reflect pressure on results. Qualifications: Set placement may reflect earlier attainment shaped by out-of-school factors; setting may follow rather than cause differences; some working-class pupils reach top sets. The data also come from official statistics of 400 pupils aged 12 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 50 and 32; 1 mark for 18 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes reluctance to take on loans for higher education, more common among working-class students?
items.answer: Fear of debt
items.markingKey: Fear of debt: reluctance to take on loans for higher education, more common among working-class students. [1]

items.stem: Briefly explain Howard’s view that poorer pupils have lower intakes of energy, vitamins and minerals, which affects health and concentration.
items.answer: Howard found young people from poorer homes had poorer diets, leading to more absence and difficulty concentrating.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Howard found young people from poorer homes had poorer diets, leading to more absence and difficulty concentrating. [2]

items.stem: Explain Reay’s argument that working-class students are more likely to apply to local universities to reduce costs, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Reay found working-class students chose universities close to home, limiting their options, partly because of costs and fear of debt. Criticism: Cultural factors and confidence also shape choices, not only money.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A secondary school in Manila finds that pupils eligible for free meals miss more school trips and have higher absence rates. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: education performs vital functions for society: it passes on shared values and creates social solidarity (Durkheim), acts as a bridge from particularistic family values to universalistic values of wider society, and allocates people to roles on the basis of merit (Parsons, Davis and Moore).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Ana, a sociology student, is designing a project on working-class students’ decisions about university. Evaluate the use of personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they may be the only source of evidence about the past. Limitations: they are usually unrepresentative because only some people keep or publish them; their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying working-class students’ decisions about university but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: The table shows exam results for 500 pupils in Lima, by eligibility for free school meals. Table: percentage achieving five good passes at age 16 | 2015 | 2025. Pupils eligible for free school meals | 41% | 45%. Other pupils | 70% | 69%. (a) Calculate the percentage change in the figure for Pupils eligible for free school meals between 2015 and 2025. Show your working. (b) Explain one limitation of using official statistics to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that material deprivation is the main cause of class differences in achievement.
items.answer: (a) (45 − 41) ÷ 41 × 100 = 9.8%. (b) They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Pupils eligible for free school meals; the figure fell for Other pupils; Other pupils had the highest figure for 2025. Cultural capital differences between classes (Bourdieu). Qualifications: Free school meal eligibility is only a rough measure of class; cultural and in-school factors also matter; some poor pupils achieve highly. The data also come from official statistics of 500 pupils aged 16 in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for (45 − 41) ÷ 41 × 100; 1 mark for 9.8% (accept 2-3 s.f.). [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes Bourdieu’s term for the dispositions, tastes and ways of thinking learnt through socialisation in a particular class?
items.answer: Habitus
items.markingKey: Habitus: Bourdieu’s term for the dispositions, tastes and ways of thinking learnt through socialisation in a particular class. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A revision guide states: “Cultural deprivation theory has been criticised for blaming the victim.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain what Bourdieu meant by cultural capital and how it affects achievement.
items.answer: (a) Correct. It locates the problem in working-class families rather than in the education system or inequality. (b) Cultural capital is the knowledge, attitudes, language and tastes of the middle class; schools value these, so middle-class pupils fit in and succeed while working-class pupils are disadvantaged; success appears to be due to merit.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2] (b) 1 mark definition; 1 mark link to school values; 1 mark effect on achievement/legitimation. [3]

items.stem: Explain two criticisms of cultural deprivation theory.
items.answer: It blames the victim and ignores material deprivation; working-class culture is different, not deficient (Keddie); working-class parents value education but face practical barriers (Blackstone and Mortimore); it ignores school factors such as labelling.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A survey of 300 pupils aged 15 in Lagos produced the data below. Table: percentage achieving high grades in an English exam | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Pupils who read for pleasure daily | 78% | 67%. Pupils who never read for pleasure | 61% | 54%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Pupils who never read for pleasure (Working-class pupils minus Middle-class pupils)?
items.answer: -7 percentage points
items.markingKey: 54 − 61 = -7 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of cultural capital and achievement (1200 pupils aged 15, Kuala Lumpur). Table: percentage achieving high grades in an English exam | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Pupils who read for pleasure daily | 73% | 68%. Pupils who never read for pleasure | 55% | 41%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for Working-class pupils. (b) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Pupils who never read for pleasure.
items.answer: (a) Pupils who read for pleasure daily (68%). (b) 41 − 55 = -14 percentage points (Working-class pupils compared with Middle-class pupils).
items.markingKey: (a) Pupils who read for pleasure daily, 68%. [1] (b) 1 mark for using 55 and 41; 1 mark for 14 percentage points with direction. [2]

items.stem: Amara’s parents in Manila, both university lecturers, take her to museums, discuss news at dinner and help her choose challenging books. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: education performs vital functions for society: it passes on shared values and creates social solidarity (Durkheim), acts as a bridge from particularistic family values to universalistic values of wider society, and allocates people to roles on the basis of merit (Parsons, Davis and Moore).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using participant observation to research the influence of parents’ cultural activities on children’s achievement.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth. Limitations: it cannot measure the extent of a pattern across a whole society; the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the influence of parents’ cultural activities on children’s achievement but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a prediction that comes true because people act on it?
items.answer: Self-fulfilling prophecy
items.markingKey: Self-fulfilling prophecy: a prediction that comes true because people act on it. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “educational triage”?
items.answer: Sorting pupils into those who will pass anyway, those who can be helped to pass and hopeless cases.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: sorting pupils into those who will pass anyway, those who can be helped to pass and hopeless cases. [1]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by educational triage and why it occurs.
items.answer: Teachers sort pupils into those who will pass, those who might pass with help and those seen as hopeless, focusing resources on the middle group; it occurs because league table and target pressures reward borderline improvements (Gillborn and Youdell).
items.markingKey: 1 mark definition; 1 mark three groups; 1 mark link to league tables/targets. [3]

items.stem: A survey of 1200 pupils aged 12 in Nairobi produced the data below. Table: percentage of pupils placed in each mathematics set | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Top set | 44% | 24%. Middle set | 31% | 36%. Bottom set | 25% | 40%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Bottom set (Working-class pupils minus Middle-class pupils)?
items.answer: +15 percentage points
items.markingKey: 40 − 25 = +15 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A survey of 240 pupils aged 12 in Singapore produced the data below. Table: percentage of pupils placed in each mathematics set | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Top set | 41% | 18%. Middle set | 30% | 28%. Bottom set | 29% | 54%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Top set. (b) Calculate the difference between Top set and Bottom set for Middle-class pupils and for Working-class pupils, and state for which of these the difference is larger.
items.answer: (a) 18 − 41 = -23 percentage points (Working-class pupils compared with Middle-class pupils). (b) Middle-class pupils: 12 percentage points; Working-class pupils: 36 percentage points; the difference is larger for Working-class pupils.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 41 and 18; 1 mark for 23 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark each difference (12 and 36); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3]

items.stem: A school in Santiago places pupils into sets in their first week, largely on the basis of a short test and teachers’ impressions; most pupils in the bottom set are from the poorest housing estate. Explain how a Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: labelling reflects and reproduces wider class inequality: teachers’ judgements are shaped by middle-class norms, and policies such as league tables encourage triage that disadvantages working-class pupils.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]
